name: Rosalind 'Roz' Keane
equipment: .32 pocket pistol, 8 rounds loaded, in her handbag under a compact and a press card
Press card: LOS ANGELES EVENING COURIER - R. KEANE - CITY DESK
Camera with flashbulbs (a Speed Graphic borrowed permanently from the photo desk) and 6 flashbulbs
Steno pad full of shorthand nobody else can read
A deck of cards, marked, and a deck of cards, not marked; she knows which is which by touch
Nickels for the payphone, a whole roll
A key to the Courier's newspaper morgue, which she is not supposed to have
A 1937 Courier clipping with Abel Kurland's byline, folded small
features: Knows the Block (City-Born origin: +2 Dexterity, +1 Charisma. In Los Angeles she knows every alley and whose bar is whose; advantage on Streetwise checks to find a person, place or service in the city, and once per foot chase the GM gives her pursuer the next complication)

Press Pass (with her press card in her hatband she gets into crime scenes, press boxes, courtrooms, City Hall corridors and the coroner's waiting room; a source she promises not to name is never burned through her, and she has advantage on Persuasion to get someone to talk off the record)

The Morgue (her Research checks take half the usual time; once per long rest, a call to the city desk or an hour in the newspaper morgue gives her one fact the Courier has printed about a named person, business or address, with no roll)

Ink by the Barrel (when she threatens to print what she knows about someone with a reputation to protect, she can use INT instead of CHA for Intimidation, with advantage; if he's the wrong man, Heat rises by 1 either way)
Back Room Game (Card Sharp background: she can always find a card game in town, get into it, and learn who in the room owes money and to whom; the Friday press-room game owes her favours)

personality.traits: I talk fast, I write faster, and I never stop asking the next question. I call everyone 'honey' because it makes them underestimate me, and it works every time.
personality.ideals: The public has a right to know, and I have a right to tell them first.
personality.bonds: Abel Kurland was my first city editor. He taught me that a good lead is a fact with its coat off. He went to the pictures in 1940 and I never forgave him for it, and I never told him he was the best newspaperman I ever knew.
personality.flaws: I'd sell my own mother for a front page, and I'd feel bad about it afterwards, and I'd do it again.

appearance: Thirty, small, quick, freckled, with red hair pinned up under a hat that has seen better newsrooms and a pencil through it like a hatpin. Ink on her fingers, a run in her stocking, a laugh you can hear across a press room.
backstory: Roz Keane grew up over her father's tailor shop in Boyle Heights, learned Yiddish from the neighbours and poker from her father's customers, and talked her way onto the Evening Courier as a copy girl in 1936. Abel Kurland, then the city editor, sent her to cover a fire because nobody else was in the room, and she came back with the fire chief's confession that the building had been condemned for two years. She has been on the city desk since, covering the courts, the cops and lately the committee's investigators. Her editor will spike anything about Castellane Pictures because the Courier's publisher plays golf with Bernard Castellane. She knows something nobody else does: on Monday 15 September, over a drink at a counter on the boulevard, Kurland told her, 'Roz, I've got the whole city council in a film can.' She thought it was a pitch for a picture.
